title: Quentin and the Bell
premise: Edmund Halloran, a late-night radio host in the fading town of Marrow Creek, begins receiving calls from listeners who died the week before — and among them is a voice describing a debt from 1974 that Edmund's family never paid. When Quentin, Edmund's childhood imaginary friend, appears on the porch unchanged after thirty years, she becomes the only living bridge between the dead callers and whatever took them. Together they uncover that Edmund's grandfather led a vigilante drowning of an innocent man in 1974, and the town's dead have been waiting for restitution ever since. To save the remaining townsfolk, Edmund must publicly confess the buried crime, return the drowned man's stolen belongings to his last living kin, and accept that justice outside the law may cost Edmund the radio show, the family name, and nearly their life.
about_author: Elodie Zhou is a former small-town radio producer who spent six years archiving call-in tapes before turning to fiction. She writes horror rooted in rural communities, where old debts outlive everyone who incurred them.

chapters.title: The Dead Air Line
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. During a routine broadcast, a caller describes her own funeral from last Tuesday; Edmund assumes a prank but can't shake the voice's familiarity. The chapter establishes the show, the lonely studio, and Edmund's habit of explaining away the unexplainable. Emotional beat: unease disguised as professionalism.

chapters.title: Second Caller
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. A second dead listener calls, naming Edmund by childhood nickname no one alive uses. Edmund checks obituaries, finds both callers confirmed deceased, and records the calls as evidence against their own disbelief. Emotional beat: the first crack in fifteen years of rational armor.

chapters.title: The Porch
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Arriving at Edmund's house at dusk, Quentin — who hasn't existed since she was eight — waits on the porch, unchanged, holding a rusted key. Edmund recognizes her instantly and neither speaks of what that means. Emotional beat: uncanny tenderness, the return of something loved and impossible.

chapters.title: What Imaginary Friends Remember
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin explains she was never imaginary; she was sent to watch over Edmund's family until a debt was settled, and the settling is overdue. She doesn't know the details — only the year: 1974. Emotional beat: wonder curdling into obligation.

chapters.title: The Attic Boxes
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Searching the family attic, Edmund finds a locked footlocker matching Quentin's key, containing a man's wallet, a wedding ring, and a newspaper clipping about a drowning ruled accidental. Emotional beat: dread of inheritance, the past made physical.

chapters.title: Third Voice
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. On air, a third dead caller recites the drowning victim's name — Daniel Okafor — and says 'he counts you every night.' The station manager warns Edmund about ratings and rumors. Emotional beat: public pressure tightening around private terror.

chapters.title: Marrow Creek Remembers Differently
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin walks Edmund through town, pointing where buildings stood in 1974 and interviewing elderly residents who go silent or lie badly when Daniel's name surfaces. Emotional beat: a town's complicity felt street by street.

chapters.title: The Grandfather's Ledger
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. In the footlocker's false bottom, Edmund finds a ledger listing seven names — the men present at the drowning — including Edmund's grandfather. Six are crossed out; each died within the last month. Emotional beat: horror becoming arithmetic, one name left.

chapters.title: The Last Name
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. The seventh name is Edmund's father, still alive in a care home, nonverbal after a stroke. Visiting him, Edmund finds Daniel's ring clutched in his hand for decades. Emotional beat: grief for a parent who may have been a perpetrator.

chapters.title: Quentin's Rule
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Quentin reveals her purpose: she was bound to the family to ensure return of what was taken, and if it isn't returned by the anniversary night, the debt collects 'in kind' — a life for a life, starting with Edmund. Emotional beat: love expressed as a deadline.

chapters.title: Finding the Kin
chapters.summary: Both POVs alternating. They trace Daniel Okafor's family to a granddaughter, Ruth, living two counties away, who has her own file of unanswered questions about her grandfather's 'accident.' Emotional beat: cautious alliance between strangers sharing a wound.

chapters.title: Ruth's Terms
chapters.summary: Ruth's POV. Ruth agrees to meet but demands the full truth first, not ritual or apology. Edmund confesses the family's role aloud for the first time and feels both lighter and exposed. Emotional beat: confession as beginning, not absolution.

chapters.title: The Anniversary Approaches
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Strange signs multiply: dead birds facing the river, phones ringing with river sounds, Quentin flickering at the edges like bad reception. The radio dead grow more insistent, broadcasting through car stereos across town. Emotional beat: escalating siege atmosphere.

chapters.title: The Town Turns
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV. Descendants of the six dead men confront Edmund, blaming them for waking 'it,' and vandalize the station. Edmund realizes the town would rather bury the truth again than be saved by it. Emotional beat: isolation sharpening into resolve.

chapters.title: What the River Kept
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. At the drowning site, Quentin shows Edmund the memory she's carried since 1974: Daniel didn't struggle; he forgave them as he went under, and that forgiveness is what the debt refuses to accept. Emotional beat: sorrow deeper than fear.

chapters.title: The Plan
chapters.summary: Both POVs. Edmund decides to confess live on air — naming the seven, returning the wallet and ring to Ruth publicly, on the anniversary night itself. Ruth will speak for Daniel. Quentin warns the dead must hear it from the family bloodline. Emotional beat: terrified determination.

chapters.title: Sabotage
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Townsfolk cut the station's power and steal the footlocker. Quentin retrieves it from the riverbank at great cost, fading badly, while Edmund broadcasts the first half of the confession on battery power to whoever can still hear. Emotional beat: sacrifice and scrambling hope.

chapters.title: The Broadcast
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, climax part one. Live on the anniversary night, Edmund names every man, reads the ledger, and gives the ring to Ruth on air. The dead callers listen in silence; then all lines light up at once. Emotional beat: catharsis under maximum danger.

chapters.title: In Kind
chapters.summary: Quentin's POV, climax part two. The debt demands its life anyway — the river rises into the studio — and Quentin offers herself, the watcher, as payment in Edmund's place. Edmund refuses to let go of her hand as the water takes its measure. Emotional beat: love against the arithmetic.

chapters.title: Settled
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Dawn: the water recedes, the calls stop, and Quentin is gone — not erased, but released, leaving the key behind. Ruth stays in touch; the town says nothing, but some doors that were closed begin to open. Emotional beat: exhausted, incomplete peace.

chapters.title: Sign-Off
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV. Weeks later, Edmund ends the final broadcast by reading Daniel Okafor's name into the record and resigning, handing the frequency to a community board. Justice outside the law cost everything except the truth. Emotional beat: quiet reckoning.

chapters.title: The Porch Light
chapters.summary: Edmund's POV, coda. On the porch at dusk, a child's laughter — or maybe just wind — and the key warm in Edmund's pocket. Some watchers choose to stay. Emotional beat: found family persisting beyond death, hope with teeth.
